claims.claim: The goal is inner calm: not being ruled or stirred by strong feelings.

stances.summary: The perfect Christian should be free of every passion of the soul, not merely moderate in them. Having God by love, he no longer needs even the feelings people call good, such as courage, cheerfulness or zeal.
stances.quote: We must therefore rescue the gnostic and perfect man from all passion of the soul. For knowledge (gnosis) produces practice, and practice habit or disposition; and such a state as this produces impassibility, not moderation of passion.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885
stances.context: The chapter's own heading is 'The Gnostic Free of All Perturbations of the Soul'. Clement says Christ 'was entirely impassible; inaccessible to any movement of feeling, either pleasure or pain', and that the apostles after the resurrection were not moved even by 'courage, zeal, joy, desire'. He explicitly rejects the objection that anger and desire are needed to fight evil or to long for the good: love already possesses what desire seeks. He denies the perfect man even 'gladness' and 'dejection', and 'high spirit'. Bodily needs such as hunger and thirst remain. Written in Alexandria about 200. 'Gnostic' is his word for the mature Christian, not the heretical sects he opposed. This is the plainest statement of the claim in the whole early Church, and the root of the later monastic ideal of apatheia (dispassion). The Greek was not checked for this file.

stances.summary: The kingdom of heaven is a soul at peace from its passions, together with true knowledge. The whole monastic struggle aims at dispassion, and love is born from it.
stances.quote: The kingdom of heaven is dispassion of the soul, together with true knowledge of the things that exist.
stances.translation: Own literal rendering from the Greek (the only English versions, Bamberger 1970, Sinkewicz 2003 and Dysinger, are copyrighted)
stances.original: Βασιλεια ουρανων εστιν απαθεια ψυχης μετα γνωσεως των οντνων αληθους
stances.work: Praktikos (The Monk: A Treatise on the Practical Life)
stances.context: The Greek above is copied exactly as the url page prints it: without accents and with a typo (οντνων). The standard reading is 'Βασιλεία οὐρανῶν ἐστιν ἀπάθεια ψυχῆς μετὰ γνώσεως τῶν ὄντων ἀληθοῦς'. The url page also carries Luke Dysinger's own English, which is copyrighted and was not copied. On the same page, chapter 81 (own rendering): love is the offspring of dispassion, and dispassion is the flower of the practical life (Greek begins 'Ἀπαθείας ἔγγονον ἀγάπη'). Chapter 64 gives as signs of dispassion a mind that stays quiet even before images in sleep and looks at things calmly. Evagrius's dispassion is not numbness: chapter 24 says the natural use of anger (thymos) is to fight the demons, and that the demons twist it, against its nature, into fighting people. Written in the Egyptian desert in the 390s. HETERODOX STATUS: Evagrius was condemned with Origen in the sixth century (the Origenist condemnations around the Council of Constantinople in 553), though his practical teaching passed into Eastern monasticism through Cassian and the Philokalia, often under other names. Jerome attacked his apatheia by name in Letter 133 (see Jerome).

stances.summary: Anger must be rooted out completely, even anger with a good reason. The goal of patience is not to be angry rightly but never to be angry at all.
stances.quote: For the end and aim of patience consists, not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all.
stances.translation: Edgar C. S. Gibson, NPNF series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.location: Book 8 (on the spirit of anger), chapter 21
stances.context: Written in Gaul about 420, passing on what he learned among the Egyptian monks (and, silently, from Evagrius). The whole of Book 8 argues it. Chapter 5, headed 'How calm a monk ought to be', says Paul's 'Let all anger be taken away' 'excepts none whatever as necessary or useful for us'. Chapter 21 argues that the words 'without a cause' in Matthew 5:22 are a later addition 'by those who did not think that anger for just causes was to be banished'. Chapter 22: 'we ought never to be angry at all, whether for good or bad reasons'. Chapter 19 confesses he once raged at his pen and penknife when alone in the desert. The single exception he allows (chapter 7): anger turned against one's own sinful impulses. In the Conferences the monk's immediate goal is 'purity of heart', his Latin for Evagrius's apatheia. Cassian's teaching on grace was later criticised in the West as 'semi-Pelagian', which does not touch this point.

stances.summary: After twenty years alone, his soul was neither shrunk by grief nor loosened by pleasure. He was not troubled by the crowd or overjoyed by praise, but steady and guided by reason.
stances.quote: for it was neither contracted as if by grief, nor relaxed by pleasure, nor possessed by laughter or dejection, for he was not troubled when he beheld the crowd, nor overjoyed at being saluted by so many. But he was altogether even as being guided by reason, and abiding in a natural state.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF series 2 vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: This is Athanasius's description of Antony emerging from about twenty years of solitude (about 305), written about 357, a year or two after Antony's death, by a bishop who says he knew him. It is a portrait, not Antony's own sentence. Antony's own words in the long sermon the Life gives him (chapter 36) point the same way: fear, confusion and grief come from the demons, while 'joy and a settled state of soul show the holiness of him who is present'. Note that his calm is joyful, not blank: chapter 67 says 'he was never disturbed, for his soul was at peace; he was never downcast, for his mind was joyous'. John Climacus (Ladder, step 29) cites 'the Egyptian' who said he no longer feared the Lord as a sign of dispassion.

stances.summary: He held up Antony's untroubled soul as the model of holiness: a peaceful soul shows in a calm, cheerful face.
stances.quote: For as his soul was free from disturbances, his outward appearance was calm; so from the joy of his soul he possessed a cheerful countenance
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF series 2 vol. 4, 1892
stances.context: Athanasius's own narrating voice (about 357), praising the state as the fruit of holiness and a gift 'from the Saviour'. He wrote the Life as a pattern for monks. Counted separately from Antony because this is the author's own ideal, but it is the same evidence; weight it lightly. The calm he praises is joyful: 'he was never downcast, for his mind was joyous'.

stances.summary: He was always the same: no one ever saw him angry, stirred up, grieving or laughing. A kind of heavenly gladness showed in his face instead.
stances.quote: No one ever saw him enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing; he was always one and the same: displaying a kind of heavenly happiness in his countenance, he seemed to have passed the ordinary limits of human nature.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts, NPNF series 2 vol. 11, 1894
stances.original: Nemo umquam illum vidit iratum, nemo commotum, nemo maerentem, nemo ridentem: unus idemque fuit semper, caelestem quodammodo laetitiam vultu praeferens extra, naturam hominis videbatur.
stances.work: Life of St Martin (by Sulpicius Severus)
stances.context: A portrait by his disciple Sulpicius Severus, who visited him and wrote about 396, while Martin was still alive. No writings of Martin survive, so this is the best evidence of his ideal, but it is a biographer's picture. The next lines qualify it: 'Frequently, too, he used to weep for the sins of those who showed themselves his revilers', so the unmoved man still wept, for others' sins. Latin from The Latin Library, https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/sulpiciusseverusmartin.html (punctuation as printed there).

stances.summary: If you want to see the truth clearly, drive out joy, fear, hope and grief. A mind ruled by these is chained and blind.
stances.quote: Joy, hope and fear Suffer not near, Drive grief away: Shackled and blind And lost is the mind Where these have sway.
stances.translation: H. R. James, 1897 (Project Gutenberg ebook 14328)
stances.location: Book 1, poem 7 (headed "The Perturbations of Passion" in this translation)
stances.context: The page sets this as verse; the quote runs the lines together (line breaks collapsed to spaces). Spoken by Lady Philosophy, the authoritative voice of the book, closing Book 1, in which she diagnoses the prisoner's 'anger, pain, and grief' as 'tumultuous passions' to be healed first by gentle and then by sharper remedies. The whole book is a cure of grief by reason. Written in prison in Pavia about 524, awaiting execution. The Consolation never names Christ; Boethius was a Christian and wrote theological treatises on the Trinity, and the book was read as a Christian classic for a thousand years. The Latin (Book 1, metre 7) was not checked for this file.

stances.summary: Dispassion is heaven on earth: a heaven of the mind inside the heart, where the tricks of the demons now look like toys. It is the second-highest rung of the ladder, just below love.
stances.quote: For I take dispassion to be nothing other than a heaven of the mind within the heart, which from now on counts the tricks of the demons as toys.
stances.translation: Own literal rendering from the Greek of Migne's Patrologia Graeca 88 as transcribed on Greek Wikisource (the usual English, Moore 1959 and Luibheid and Russell 1982, is copyrighted)
stances.original: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἕτερόν τι ἔγωγε ἀπάθειαν ὑπείληφα εἶναι· ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ἐγκάρδιον νοὸς οὐρανὸν, τὰς τῶν δαιμόνων πανουργίας, ἀθύρματα λοιπὸν λογιζόμενον.
stances.context: Written at Sinai in the seventh century. Step 29 is titled (own rendering) On the earthly heaven, godlike dispassion and perfection, and the resurrection of the soul before the general resurrection; only step 30, on faith, hope and love, stands above it. The same step says 'the Egyptian' showed dispassion when he said he no longer feared the Lord, and it defines long-suffering as staying calm (γαληνιᾷν) whether the one who insults you is present or absent. Qualification: Climacus's dispassion is not dry-eyed. Step 7 is 'On joy-making mourning' (Περὶ τοῦ χαροποιοῦ πένθους), and tears of compunction run through the whole book, so he is the clearest case of calm and tears held together.

stances.summary: Anger, fear, desire and the like are not the soul itself but growths on it, like warts. Reason should rule them as tools for now, and the soul loses nothing when it is finally free of them.
stances.quote: It will therefore be no detriment to our participation in the Good, that the soul should be free from such emotions, and turning back upon herself should know herself accurately what her actual nature is
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF series 2 vol. 5, 1893
stances.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection (dialogue written by her brother Gregory of Nyssa)
stances.location: Macrina speaking, in the passage on why desire will cease when the soul reaches the Good
stances.context: Gregory wrote the dialogue soon after her death (379 or 380) and gives her the role of 'the Teacher'. It opens with her checking his grief for Basil, quoting Paul on not grieving 'like men without hope'. She calls anger, desire, fear, pleasure and pain 'not the soul, but only like warts growing out of the soul's thinking part', and holds up Moses as free of both anger and desire. HER QUALIFICATION: in this life she treats the emotions as neutral instruments: 'fear will only generate within us obedience, and anger fortitude', if reason 'holds the dominion', and she warns that uprooting desire and anger altogether would leave us nothing to rise to God or fight evil with. So her full view is: rule them now, be free of them at the end, when only love remains. Hence strength 1. The Life of Macrina (Gregory of Nyssa, trans. W. K. Lowther Clarke, 1916) shows the same in practice: at her brother Naucratius's death 'by her own steadfastness and imperturbability [she] taught her mother's soul to be brave' (https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_macrina_1_life.htm). Gregory of Nyssa himself presents her as his teacher and does not dissent.

stances.summary: Christians should not mourn their dead: they are not lost but sent ahead. Long wailing and black clothes deny the hope we preach.
stances.quote: our brethren who are freed from this world by the Lord's summons are not to be lamented, since we know that they are not lost, but sent before
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886
stances.context: Written in Carthage during the plague of about 252. This is about one feeling (grief for the dead) and its reason is hope in the resurrection, not a philosophy of calm; so it supports the claim only in part. He adds that the dead 'should be desired, but not bewailed', and in section 7 that 'when the dear ones whom we love depart from the world, we should rather rejoice than grieve'. Cyprian also wrote On the Advantage of Patience.

stances.summary: Aim at a calm temper, but do not try to root feeling out. Reason should guide natural anger, because a person who is never roused by wrongdoing is not virtuous but apathetic.
stances.quote: The moral teacher who knew that the natural disposition should rather be guided by a reasonable course of teaching, than be eradicated, teaches morals, and says: Be angry where there is a fault against which you ought to be angry. For it is impossible not to be roused up by the baseness of many things; otherwise we might be accounted, not virtuous, but apathetic and neglectful.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF series 2 vol. 10, 1896
stances.work: On the Duties of the Clergy (De officiis)
stances.context: Written about 389 for his clergy. The same chapter (section 90) sets the other half: 'The first thing, therefore, to aim at, if possible, is to make tranquillity of character our natural disposition by constant practice', but 'since passion is to a large extent implanted in our nature... it cannot be uprooted', it must be checked by reason. On grief, in his funeral speech for his brother Satyrus (378): 'Not all weeping proceeds from unbelief or weakness. Natural grief is one thing, distrustful sadness is another', and 'I confess, then, that I too wept, but the Lord also wept' (On the Death of Satyrus 1.10, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/34031.htm); yet he ends by saying his tears must cease because believers should differ from those without hope (1.70). A deliberate middle: calm as the aim, feeling as natural and sometimes a duty.

stances.summary: A gentle calm that never burns with zeal is a fault, and so is zeal that loses gentleness. The Spirit came as a dove and as fire, and a full soul has both.
stances.quote: He then is in no wise full of the Holy Spirit, who either in the calm of meekness forsakes the fervour of zeal, or again in the ardour of zeal loses the virtue of meekness.
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF series 2 vol. 12, 1895
stances.location: Book 3, chapter 16 (Admonition 17: how the meek and the passionate are to be admonished)
stances.context: Written about 590. Just before: 'the meek, when they are in authority, suffer from the torpor of sloth'; 'the Holy Spirit has been manifested to us in a dove and in fire; because, to wit, all whom He fills He causes to show themselves as meek with the simplicity of the dove, and burning with the fire of zeal.' He also warns that the angry often mistake their rage for 'the zeal of righteousness'. So calm is praised but is not the goal on its own; a calm person is told to 'embrace solicitude'. This is the book behind the planned Personality Quiz (#1), so the two quizzes can cross-link here.

stances.summary: Grief at a terrible loss is natural, and only a stony heart would feel little. But sober reason must set limits to it, and quiet and solitude help reason bring the passions under control.
stances.quote: Who could be so stony-hearted, so truly inhuman, as to be insensible to what has occurred, or be affected by merely moderate grief?
stances.translation: Blomfield Jackson, NPNF series 2 vol. 8, 1895
stances.work: Letter 5, to Nectarius (consoling him on the death of his son)
stances.context: Basil says he 'sighed and wept' himself, then in section 2 turns to 'that sober reason which in our happy days is wont to draw lines of limitation round our souls', cites Paul's command not to grieve like those without hope, and urges: 'do not fall under the weight of your grief'. The other half of his view is Letter 2, to Gregory of Nazianzus, written from his retreat in Pontus about 358: 'solitude is of the greatest use for this purpose, inasmuch as it stills our passions, and gives room for principle to cut them out of the soul', naming 'lust and anger, fear and sorrow, the soul's deadly foes' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202002.htm). Both letters are early. On solitude itself Basil later changed his mind: his monastic Rules favour life in community (not re-checked for this file). His view on the feelings themselves does not visibly change: calm under reason, feeling not abolished.

stances.summary: Weep for the dead, but in measure. Scripture keeps us from both hardness and excess.
stances.quote: For I am neither going to lament for him who is gone more than is good— as I should not approve of such conduct even in others — nor am I going to praise him beyond due measure.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF series 2 vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 7, funeral speech for his brother Caesarius
stances.context: Delivered in 368 or 369. He goes on to cite Sirach 38:16, 'Let tears fall down over the dead, and begin to lament', as 'removing us equally from insensibility and immoderation', then turns the grief toward things eternal. In section 6 he admits his tears show that 'my feelings have overcome my philosophic restraint'. A plain middle view: measured feeling, neither numbness nor excess.

stances.summary: No human being can be free of passions; we can master them, not be rid of them. Anger is even useful at the right time, when it corrects others rather than avenges ourselves.
stances.quote: Thus He has not altogether taken the thing away: first, because it is not possible, being a man, to be freed from passions: we may indeed get the dominion over them, but to be altogether without them is out of the question. Next, because this passion is even useful, if we know how to use it at the suitable time.
stances.translation: George Prevost, revised by M. B. Riddle, NPNF series 1 vol. 10, 1888
stances.location: Homily 16, section 9 in the NPNF numbering (on Matthew 5:22)
stances.context: Preached in Antioch about 390. He goes on: 'What then is the proper time for anger? When we are not avenging ourselves, but checking others in their lawless freaks', and 'Being angry then is not a transgression, but being so unseasonably.' The same homily still presses hard against anger ('wrath is the root of murder'), and his letters from exile (404-407) labour to lift Olympias out of 'despondency' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1916.htm). So: master the passions, use anger rarely and for others, but do not dream of being without them. Mixed rather than disagree because his constant pastoral aim is calm. Contrast the famous line 'he who is not angry when he has cause, sins', which is NOT his (see misattributions).

stances.summary: Stillness and purity are the path, but purity itself is a heart full of mercy. The merciful heart burns for every creature and weeps even for demons and reptiles.
stances.quote: And what is a merciful heart? He replied: The burning of the heart unto the whole creation, man, fowls and beasts, demons and whatever exists
stances.translation: A. J. Wensinck, Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh, Amsterdam 1923
stances.location: Treatise 74 in Wensinck (p. 341); other editions number it differently
stances.context: The url is the archive.org OCR text of Wensinck's 1923 translation; the quote crosses a line break there. The answer continues: 'so that by the recollection and the sight of them the eyes shed tears on account of the force of mercy which moves the heart by great compassion', until the heart 'is not able to bear hearing or examining injury or any insignificant suffering of anything in the creation'. The same treatise opens: 'what is the sum of purity? A heart full of mercy unto the whole created nature.' Isaac puts the answers in the mouth of an unnamed Father and adopts them. Isaac (late seventh century) is the great teacher of stillness, yet here the goal of stillness is a heart that is deeply moved; that is why he is mixed and not agree. The treatise before it ends: 'as long as we are in this world... it is not possible to be free from toil and injury and care.' STATUS: a bishop of Nineveh in the Church of the East (the church outside the Byzantine communion, often called 'Nestorian'); his writings were translated into Greek and he is venerated by the Orthodox.

stances.summary: He fled to the desert to be still and taught that trials should make a man firm and unmoved. Yet he wept all his life and said the fear of death had been with him since he became a monk.
stances.quote: " The dread of this hour hath been with me in very truth from "the time when I became a monk, and was afraid."
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, Paradise, Book 1 of the Sayings)
stances.location: saying 151 (Budge numbering, Book 1 of the Sayings)
stances.context: The url is archive.org OCR, so the quote keeps its stray quotation marks exactly as printed there. Clean reading: 'The dread of this hour hath been with me in very truth from the time when I became a monk, and was afraid.' The brothers had asked him on his deathbed, 'Art thou also afraid, O father?' The other side: the voice he heard, 'Arsenius, flee, keep silence, and lead a life of silent contemplation, for these are the fundamental causes which prevent a man from committing sin' (at the start of the same book), and his saying 220 that trials burn a man like a brick 'so that he may remain firm and unmoved'. Saying 165: 'his eyelashes were destroyed by weeping'. So the great lover of stillness was not a calm man in the modern sense; his stillness held fear of God and constant tears. Died about 449.

stances.summary: Do not act on anger or nurse it, and do not love loud laughter. But fear the judgment, and confess your sins to God every day with tears and groans.
stances.quote: Not to carry anger through into action. Not to save up a time for one’s wrath.
stances.translation: Own literal rendering from the Latin (Doyle 1948 is on Project Gutenberg, but only pre-1929 English is used here)
stances.original: Iram non perficere. Iracundiæ tempus non reservare.
stances.context: The url page prints 'Iracundiæ' through an HTML entity (æ). Written about 530-540. The same list says 'Risum multum aut excussum non amare' (not to love much or boisterous laughter), and chapter 7 makes 'not easily and quickly moved to laughter' the tenth step of humility. But the list also says 'Diem iudicii timere. Gehennam expavescere' (to fear the day of judgment, to dread hell) and 'Mala sua praeterita cum lacrimis vel gemitu cotidie in oratione Deo confiteri' (daily in prayer to confess one's past sins to God with tears or groaning). The top of the ladder in chapter 7 is 'caritatem Dei... illam quae perfecta foris mittit timorem' (the love of God which, being perfect, casts out fear; own rendering), and the Prologue promises running God's way 'dilatato corde inenarrabili dilectionis dulcedine' (with heart enlarged, in the unspeakable sweetness of love; own rendering). Restraint, not numbness: the Rule governs feelings rather than removing them.

stances.summary: Christians rightly fear, desire, grieve and rejoice, and Christ Himself felt all of these. To feel nothing at all in this life would be worse than any vice.
stances.quote: And if that is to be called apathy, where the mind is the subject of no emotion, then who would not consider this insensibility to be worse than all vices?
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, NPNF series 1 vol. 2, 1887
stances.original: Porro si *a)pa/qeia illa dicenda est, cum animum contingere omnino non potest ullus affectus, quis hunc stuporem non omnibus uitiis iudicet esse peiorem?
stances.context: Written about 418-420, answering the Stoics. The chapter begins: the citizens of God's city 'both fear and desire, and grieve and rejoice. And because their love is rightly placed, all these affections of theirs are right.' He lists Christ's anger, gladness, tears and sorrow and says 'these emotions are certainly not falsely ascribed to Him', and: 'so long as we wear the infirmity of this life, we are rather worse men than better if we have none of these emotions at all.' It ends: 'For a thing is not necessarily right because it is inflexible, nor healthy because it is insensible.' HIS QUALIFICATION: freedom from emotions that fight reason is 'a good and most desirable quality, but it is not one which is attainable in this life', and in heaven there will be love and joy but no fear or grief. Earlier, in Confessions 9.12 (about 397), he had held back his tears at Monica's death and blamed 'the softness of my feelings', then wept and wrote 'if he finds me to have sinned in weeping for my mother... let him not laugh me to scorn' (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/110109.htm); by the City of God he defends such feelings outright. The Latin comes from The Latin Library (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/augustine/civ14.shtml), which writes the Greek word apatheia in Beta code as '*a)pa/qeia'.

stances.summary: God planted the emotions in us as the soil of virtue. The Stoics who want a calm, unmoved soul are asking for something impossible and wrong: still water goes stagnant, and so does a still soul.
stances.quote: while they desire to free the soul from perturbations, and, as they themselves say, to render it calm and tranquil; which is not only impossible, because its force and nature consist in motion, but it ought not even to be so. For as water which is always still and motionless is unwholesome and more muddy, so the soul which is unmoved and torpid is useless even to itself
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886
stances.context: Written about 304-311. Chapters 14 to 17 argue it at length. He calls the Stoics 'mad who do not regulate but cut them out', and says 'he who is without anger is also without virtue' (chapter 15). He rejects the Peripatetic middle way too: it is not the amount of a feeling that matters but its object, since the right joy may be great and the wrong joy wicked even when small (chapter 16). Fear of God and desire for heaven are named as the highest virtues (chapter 17). He calls feeling-free people deprived of 'humanity', since the affections are those 'in which humanity altogether consists'. His separate treatise On the Anger of God argues that God Himself is truly angry at sin. The Latin was not checked for this file.

stances.summary: The Stoic claim that we can root out grief, gladness, hope and fear takes away human nature. A mind that is never stirred is either a stone or God.
stances.quote: a state in which the mind ceases to be agitated and — to speak simply — becomes either a stone or a God.
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF series 2 vol. 6, 1893
stances.context: Written about 414-415. The line mocks Evagrius's 'book of maxims on apathy, or, as we should say, impassivity or imperturbability'. In section 1 he says the Stoic claim that the passions 'such as vexation and gladness, hope and fear' can be rooted out is 'to take man's nature from him, to forget that he is constituted of body as well as soul'. His real target is the Pelagian claim that a person can live without sin; he links apatheia to it. Jerome's own practice matched: consoling Paula on her daughter Blaesilla's death in 384 he wrote 'I make no secret of my feelings; this entire letter is written in tears', while still telling her that her grief had gone too far (Letter 39, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3001039.htm). The Latin was not checked for this file.

stances.summary: Anger and desire are not always irrational. Christ was indignant and longed to eat the Passover, and God is rightly angry at evil, so feeling guided by reason belongs to a good soul.
stances.quote: In our own cases, accordingly, the irascible and the concupiscible elements of our soul must not invariably be put to the account of the irrational (nature), since we are sure that in our Lord these elements operated in entire accordance with reason.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3, 1885
stances.original: Igitur apud nos non semper ex inrationali censenda sunt indignatiuum et concupiscentiuum, quae certi sumus in domino rationaliter decucurrisse.
stances.context: Written about 210-213, in his Montanist period (HETERODOX: Tertullian joined the New Prophecy movement, later rejected by the Church). Against Plato, he sees in Christ 'the rational element', 'indignation... by which He inveighed against the scribes and the Pharisees', and 'the principle of desire'. He adds: 'He permits us likewise to feel indignation', citing Paul's anger at the Galatian troublers. Only irrational anger, which comes from the devil, is condemned. Elsewhere, in On Patience (before his Montanist turn), he praises patience and confesses he is 'a man of no goodness' unfit to write on it. Latin from The Latin Library (https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.anima.shtml).

stances.summary: A soul at rest from its struggles has stopped growing. Ask God to give the war back, and weep over yourself in this life.
stances.quote: Go and entreat God to let war and strife "come unto thee again, for it is through war and strife that "the soul advanceth in spiritual excellence."
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge, Paradise)
stances.location: saying 215 (Budge numbering, Book 1 of the Sayings)
stances.context: The url is archive.org OCR; the quote keeps its stray quotation marks exactly. Clean reading: 'Go and entreat God to let war and strife come unto thee again, for it is through war and strife that the soul advanceth in spiritual excellence.' Poemen used to tell this story: John Colobos (John the Dwarf) prayed and his passions were taken away, and told an old man 'I perceive that my soul is at rest'; the old man answered with these words, and afterwards John never again prayed for the struggle to be removed. Poemen's own words at Arsenius's death (saying 152): 'Blessed art thou, O Abba Arsenius, for thou didst weep over thyself in this world. For he who weepeth not for himself in this world must weep for ever in the next.' And on Matthew 5:22 (saying 233): anger at one who 'wisheth to separate thee or to put thee away from God... is a good thing'. The 'passions' here mean inner temptations and struggles rather than feelings in general, so this is a qualified disagree: rest is not the goal in this life. Fifth century, Scetis. The Moses the Black sayings in Budge were checked and hold no clear position on this question.

splits_fathers: Real voices exist on both sides, and there is a large middle. FOR calm as the goal: the Alexandrian and monastic line. Clement (the perfect Christian has 'impassibility, not moderation of passion'), Evagrius (the kingdom of heaven is dispassion), Cassian (not even just anger), Climacus (dispassion is heaven on earth), the portraits of Antony (by Athanasius) and Martin (by Sulpicius), and Boethius's Lady Philosophy. AGAINST it, at least for this life: the great Latin theologians. Lactantius (the Stoic calm is madness; a still soul goes stagnant), Jerome (an unstirred mind is 'either a stone or a God') and Augustine (feeling nothing is worse than any vice; Christ grieved and was angry). Tertullian defends rational anger and desire, and in the desert Poemen says to ask for the struggle back and to weep now. THE MIDDLE, where most sit: reason rules the feelings, which are natural and sometimes a duty. Ambrose, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Chrysostom, Gregory the Great (dove and fire), Benedict (restrain anger and laughter, but weep and fear God), Macrina (rule them now, be free of them at the end), Isaac and Arsenius (stillness that weeps). Two cautions. First, even the calm camp is not dry-eyed: Antony's calm is 'joyous', Martin wept for his slanderers, Arsenius wept away his eyelashes, Climacus has a whole step on 'joy-making mourning', and Isaac makes the goal of stillness a heart that burns with mercy. Their calm is freedom from self-centred passions, not the absence of feeling. Second, nearly all of them, on every side, agree one should not be RULED by feelings. The real disagreement is whether being STIRRED (anger at wrong, grief at loss) is part of the goal or something to outgrow.
splits_people_today: The claim as worded bundles two things that split differently. 'Not being ruled by strong feelings' is close to universal today: therapy language (emotional regulation), the Stoicism revival, mindfulness and most Christian teaching on self-control all endorse it, so on its own it tells the quiz almost nothing. 'Not being stirred', calm as the goal in itself, splits people genuinely. For it: people drawn to meditation, contemplative prayer, Stoic or Buddhist-flavoured calm, 'the peace that passes understanding', and people who are even-tempered by nature. Against it: a strong modern current that prizes emotional honesty ('feel your feelings'), lament and grief work, and righteous anger at injustice. Many Christians cite Jesus weeping at Lazarus's tomb and overturning the tables, and 'be angry and sin not'. Among ordinary Christians the split is real and fairly even: activists and the emotionally expressive lean to 'stirred', contemplatives and more reserved believers lean to 'calm'. Temperament drives this as much as theology, which suits a personality-style quiz.

misattributions.line: He who is not angry when he has cause, sins. For unreasonable patience is the hotbed of many vices. (Also: 'he that is angry with cause, shall not be in danger: for without anger, teaching will be useless, judgments unstable, crimes unchecked.')
misattributions.truth: From the Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum, homily 11, an anonymous fifth-century Latin commentary by an Arian-leaning author, long printed under Chrysostom's name. Thomas Aquinas quotes it as 'Chrysostom' (Summa II-II q.158 a.1 and a.8); the New Advent edition marks it 'falsely ascribed to St. John Chrysostom' (https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3158.htm). Chrysostom's genuine Homily 16 on Matthew holds a milder view: anger 'is even useful, if we know how to use it at the suitable time'. Quote that instead.

misattributions.line: Hope has two beautiful daughters; their names are Anger and Courage.
misattributions.truth: Widely quoted online as Augustine, always without a work or chapter. It was not found in the Augustine texts read for this file, and no source for it is known. Treat it as unsourced and do not use it. (Not searched exhaustively in this pass, because web search was unavailable.)

misattributions.line: Chapters on Prayer, credited to 'St Nilus' (the source of many online lines on dispassion and pure prayer)
misattributions.truth: The Chapters on Prayer are by Evagrius Ponticus. After his condemnation they circulated under Nilus's name, including in the Philokalia and in Migne. Lines on dispassion credited online to 'St Nilus' are often Evagrius.

notes: Coverage: 23 stances from 23 people (Antony and Athanasius rest on the same book; weight Athanasius lightly). Every English quote was copied from the raw page at its url and machine-checked against a whitespace-normalised copy of that page before writing; the three own renderings (Evagrius and John Climacus from Greek, Benedict from Latin) were checked through their 'original'. Two url pages are archive.org OCR (Budge 1907 for Arsenius and Poemen; Wensinck 1923 for Isaac). Their quotes keep the OCR's stray quotation marks exactly, and the clean reading is in context. The Benedict original prints 'Iracundiæ', which the raw HTML writes as 'Iracundiæ'. Pool members looked for with no usable position found on this claim: Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Origen, Perpetua, Hippolytus, Novatian, Ephrem, Hilary, Moses the Black (his sayings in Budge are about ascetic practice, not feeling), Pelagius (Jerome's Letter 133 ties him to apatheia, but that is an opponent's report, not his own words), Paulinus of Nola, Amma Syncletica. Leads NOT verified, worth a later pass: Amma Syncletica's saying that there is a useful grief and a destructive grief (Greek alphabetical collection; she is not in Budge's Syriac collection and no pre-1929 English was found); Basil's Homily Against Anger (anger as reason's ally against sin; no pre-1929 English found); Gregory the Great's Moralia on Job 5.45 (anger through zeal versus anger through vice); Gregory of Nyssa's Homilies on the Beatitudes 2 (meekness as the realistic form of dispassion); Lactantius's On the Anger of God. Several 'agree' stances rest on biographers' portraits (Antony, Martin), not the subject's own sentence; the context says so. The most striking lines for result copy: Jerome's 'either a stone or a God'; Lactantius's still water that goes muddy; Cassian's 'not in being angry with a good reason, but in not being angry at all'; Martin never seen 'enraged, or excited, or lamenting, or laughing'; Isaac's 'burning of the heart unto the whole creation'; Poemen's story of asking God to send the war back. Natural nearest/farthest pairings: Clement or Cassian against Lactantius or Augustine. Reverent capitals: none of the chosen quotes prints a lower-case pronoun for God, so no display fix is needed here.
